newsitem.title: CONGO: Congolese president Lissouba appeals for calm.
newsitem.headline: Congolese president Lissouba appeals for calm.

text.p: Congolese President Pascal Lissouba has appealed to political leaders to halt clashes between their supporters in northern Congo which have killed 16 people in less than a month.

Supporters of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso and former prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango have clashed in the two leaders' northern home towns, Owando and Oyo, in the runup to July 27 presidential elections.
"Politicians must reconsider and distance themselves from all those who advocate senseless violence," Lissouba said on Tuesday night in a declaration carried by state media.
"What is happening in these towns is unacceptable and all those who are inciting this violence will find the government on their trail from now on," Lissouba said.
He accused politicians of importing weapons into Congo to distribute to their supporters. "Arms are being stockpiled, we have more and more evidence, and to what purpose?" he said.
Four people were shot dead in Oyo on Monday, two days after party leaders meeting in Brazzaville pledged to avoid violence in the runup to next month's election.

Shooting broke out as a convoy of vehicles belonging to Yhombi-Opango passed through Oyo, the home village of Sassou Nguesso. Twelve people were killed between May 7 and 11 in clashes in Owando, in Yhombi-Opango's home region.
Last Friday the government banned private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms, and on Saturday party leaders pledged to avoid violence in any conflict arising from the election.
Political leaders signed a declaration at a meeting attended by Lissouba and by Federico Mayor, director-general of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO).
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. The three front-runners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and opposition leader Bernard Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting following parliamentary elections in 1993 which left 2,000 dead in Brazzaville.
The militias were officially dissolved following a peace accord in 1995 but have continued to operate discreetly.
